claim: Single-molecule Förster Resonance energy transfer (smFRET) is an adaptable method for studying the structure and dynamics of biomolecules.
source: Single-molecule Förster Resonance energy transfer (smFRET) is an adaptable method for studying the structure and dynamics of biomolecules.
evidence: This is a general statement about smFRET methodology supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: DeepFRET's classification accuracy on ground truth data reached >95%.
source: Its classification accuracy on ground truth data reached >95% outperforming human operators and commonly used threshold, only requiring ~1% of the time.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental results showing classification accuracy metrics.

claim: DeepFRET outperformed human operators in classification accuracy.
source: Its classification accuracy on ground truth data reached >95% outperforming human operators and commonly used threshold, only requiring ~1% of the time.
evidence: Comparison data between DeepFRET and human operators is presented in the manuscript.

claim: DeepFRET required only ~1% of the time compared to manual methods.
source: Its classification accuracy on ground truth data reached >95% outperforming human operators and commonly used threshold, only requiring ~1% of the time.
evidence: Time comparison data is provided in the manuscript.

claim: smFRET combined with TIRFm is a key powerful method to study the structure of biomolecules and provide a dynamic perspective in structural biology.
source: Single-molecule Förster resonance energy transfer (smFRET) combined with TIRFm (total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy) is a key powerful method to study the structure of biomolecules and provide a dynamic perspective in structural biology (Lerner et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lerner et al., 2018.

claim: smFRET allows direct observations of dynamics, interactions, and intermediates of stochastic non-accumulating events.
source: Capturing the real-time readouts of nanometer-scale distances of individual biomolecules by smFRET allows the direct observations of dynamics, interactions, and intermediates of stochastic non-accumulating events, as well as dynamic equilibria between unsynchronized molecules, all of which are obscured in ensemble averaging techniques (Dimura et al., 2016; Hellenkamp et al., 2018; Holmstrom et al., 2019; Juette et al., 2016; Newton et al., 2019; Preus et al., 2015; Roy et al., 2008; Schuler and Eaton, 2008; Stella et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Ensemble averaging techniques obscure dynamics, interactions, and intermediates of stochastic non-accumulating events.
source: Capturing the real-time readouts of nanometer-scale distances of individual biomolecules by smFRET allows the direct observations of dynamics, interactions, and intermediates of stochastic non-accumulating events, as well as dynamic equilibria between unsynchronized molecules, all of which are obscured in ensemble averaging techniques (Dimura et al., 2016; Hellenkamp et al., 2018; Holmstrom et al., 2019; Juette et al., 2016; Newton et al., 2019; Preus et al., 2015; Roy et al., 2008; Schuler and Eaton, 2008; Stella et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: smFRET has been established as a key toolbox for the accurate characterization of mechanisms, biomolecular interactions function, and structures of biomolecules.
source: The high fidelity and proficiency of smFRET established it as a key toolbox for the accurate characterization of mechanisms, biomolecular interactions function, and even structures of biomolecules (Craggs and Kapanidis, 2012; Dulin et al., 2018; Kalinin et al., 2012; Kilic et al., 2018; Ratzke et al., 2014), under both in vitro (Schluesche et al., 2007; Sharma et al., 2008; Stein et al., 2011) and in vivo (Okamoto et al., 2020; Sakon and Weninger, 2010) conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: smFRET can be used under both in vitro and in vivo conditions.
source: The high fidelity and proficiency of smFRET established it as a key toolbox for the accurate characterization of mechanisms, biomolecular interactions function, and even structures of biomolecules (Craggs and Kapanidis, 2012; Dulin et al., 2018; Kalinin et al., 2012; Kilic et al., 2018; Ratzke et al., 2014), under both in vitro (Schluesche et al., 2007; Sharma et al., 2008; Stein et al., 2011) and in vivo (Okamoto et al., 2020; Sakon and Weninger, 2010) conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work demonstrating both in vitro and in vivo applications.

claim: smFRET data treatment for extracting quantitative dynamic information relies on multiple layers of preprocessing: raw image treatment, trace selection, and data analysis.
source: Despite its great quantitative utility and profound impact on structural biology, smFRET is not a direct imaging modality and data treatment for extracting quantitative dynamic information relies on multiple layers of preprocessing: raw image treatment, trace selection, and data analysis.
evidence: This describes the established workflow in smFRET analysis based on common knowledge in the field.

claim: Raw image treatment and data analysis of selected smFRET traces is in general well-standardized and relies on well-defined methodologies with strong theoretical backing.
source: Raw image treatment (Greenfeld et al., 2012; Hon and Gonzalez, 2019; Juette et al., 2016; Preus et al., 2015; Stella et al., 2018) and data analysis of the selected smFRET traces is in general well-standardized and relies on well-defined methodologies with strong theoretical backing (Hon and Gonzalez, 2019; Schmid et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published methodologies.

claim: Trace selection can be time-consuming but crucial due to the presence of undesired phenomena at the single-molecule scale.
source: The actual trace selection can be time-consuming but crucial due to the presence of undesired phenomena at the single-molecule scale, such as sample aggregation, fluorescent contaminants, incomplete or incorrect sample labeling, complex photophysical behaviors, and high noise, to mention a few (Algar et al., 2019; Hellenkamp et al., 2018; Roy et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations describing challenges in smFRET analysis.

claim: Undesired phenomena at the single-molecule scale include sample aggregation, fluorescent contaminants, incomplete or incorrect sample labeling, complex photophysical behaviors, and high noise.
source: The actual trace selection can be time-consuming but crucial due to the presence of undesired phenomena at the single-molecule scale, such as sample aggregation, fluorescent contaminants, incomplete or incorrect sample labeling, complex photophysical behaviors, and high noise, to mention a few (Algar et al., 2019; Hellenkamp et al., 2018; Roy et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations describing challenges in smFRET analysis.

claim: Existing software by single-molecule labs can simplify the tedious and time-consuming selection of traces.
source: Existing software (Greenfeld et al., 2012; Hellenkamp et al., 2018; Hon and Gonzalez, 2019; Juette et al., 2016; Preus et al., 2015; Stella et al., 2018) by single-molecule labs can simplify the tedious and time-consuming selection of traces and were recently expanded to large datasets (Juette et al., 2016) albeit requiring some form of manual supervision and hyper-parameter tuning selecting the proper thresholds by an expert user.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to existing software packages.

claim: Existing smFRET software requires some form of manual supervision and hyper-parameter tuning by an expert user.
source: Existing software (Greenfeld et al., 2012; Hellenkamp et al., 2018; Hon and Gonzalez, 2019; Juette et al., 2016; Preus et al., 2015; Stella et al., 2018) by single-molecule labs can simplify the tedious and time-consuming selection of traces and were recently expanded to large datasets (Juette et al., 2016) albeit requiring some form of manual supervision and hyper-parameter tuning selecting the proper thresholds by an expert user.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and describes limitations of existing software.

claim: Human intervention in smFRET analysis could potentially be subjected to cognitive biases especially by less experienced users.
source: This need for human intervention could potentially be subjected to cognitive biases especially by less experienced users and could limit the expansion of smFRET to classic biology labs.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the potential for bias in manual analysis.

claim: The need for human intervention could limit the expansion of smFRET to classic biology labs.
source: This need for human intervention could potentially be subjected to cognitive biases especially by less experienced users and could limit the expansion of smFRET to classic biology labs.
evidence: This is a logical inference about barriers to adoption of smFRET methodology.

claim: The increasing expansion of smFRET to structural biology labs would benefit from rapid and benchmarked methodologies, reproducible across laboratories, with minimal human intervention.
source: The increasing expansion of smFRET to structural biology labs would benefit from rapid and benchmarked methodologies, reproducible across laboratories, with minimal human intervention.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the needs of the field.

claim: Several initiatives exist to standardize the smFRET field.
source: This is highlighted by several initiatives to standardize the smFRET field (Greenfeld et al., 2012; Hellenkamp et al., 2018; Lerner et al., 2018; Sali et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to standardization initiatives.

claim: Recent advances in machine learning and specifically deep learning have radically improved our capacity to access and extract information from abstract and noisy inputs independently of human interventions.
source: Recent advances in machine learning (ML) and specifically deep learning (DL) (LeCun et al., 2015), have radically improved our capacity to access and extract information from abstract and noisy inputs independently of human interventions as we (ATLAS collaboration, 2014) and others have shown (Berg et al., 2019; Christiansen et al., 2018; Falk et al., 2019; Gómez-García et al., 2018; Jones, 2019; Ouyang et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published work on machine learning applications.

claim: DL implementations have been successfully used to analyze and augment a wide range of the fluorescence microscopy analysis pipeline.
source: DL implementations are providing high-level robust performances and have been successfully used to analyze and augment a wide range of the fluorescence microscopy analysis pipeline including assessing microscope image quality (Yang et al., 2018), in-silico cell labeling (Christiansen et al., 2018), single-cell morphology analysis (Berg et al., 2019; Falk et al., 2019), detecting single molecules (White et al., 2020; Wu and Rifkin, 2015) and linking smFRET experiments with molecular dynamics simulations (Matsunaga and Sugita, 2018), amongst others (Berg et al., 2019; Christiansen et al., 2018; Falk et al., 2019; Gómez-García et al., 2018; Jones, 2019; Ouyang et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published applications of deep learning in microscopy.

claim: Deep learning recognizes abstract patterns and learns useful features directly from the raw input data.
source: Deep learning-based analysis has several advantages over other approaches: It recognizes abstract patterns and learns useful features directly from the raw input data, which allows the implementation of analysis routines that do not require extensive data preprocessing or empirically defined rules, and thus offer reproducible and less opinionated evaluation of single-molecule data
evidence: This describes a fundamental property of deep learning based on established knowledge in machine learning.

claim: Deep learning-based analysis does not require extensive data preprocessing or empirically defined rules.
source: It recognizes abstract patterns and learns useful features directly from the raw input data, which allows the implementation of analysis routines that do not require extensive data preprocessing or empirically defined rules, and thus offer reproducible and less opinionated evaluation of single-molecule data
evidence: This describes an advantage of deep learning based on established knowledge in machine learning.

claim: Deep learning is significantly faster than human annotation for large single-molecule datasets.
source: It is significantly faster than human annotation for large single-molecule datasets; it comes close to, or outperforms human performance; and its performance is increased when increasing dataset size constituting an ideal case for evaluating the large datasets obtained from single-molecule data (Berg et al., 2019; Christiansen et al., 2018; Falk et al., 2019; Gómez-García et al., 2018; Jones, 2019; Ouyang et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work demonstrating deep learning performance.

claim: Deep learning comes close to, or outperforms human performance.
source: It is significantly faster than human annotation for large single-molecule datasets; it comes close to, or outperforms human performance; and its performance is increased when increasing dataset size constituting an ideal case for evaluating the large datasets obtained from single-molecule data (Berg et al., 2019; Christiansen et al., 2018; Falk et al., 2019; Gómez-García et al., 2018; Jones, 2019; Ouyang et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work demonstrating deep learning performance.

claim: Deep learning performance is increased when increasing dataset size.
source: It is significantly faster than human annotation for large single-molecule datasets; it comes close to, or outperforms human performance; and its performance is increased when increasing dataset size constituting an ideal case for evaluating the large datasets obtained from single-molecule data (Berg et al., 2019; Christiansen et al., 2018; Falk et al., 2019; Gómez-García et al., 2018; Jones, 2019; Ouyang et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published work and describes a fundamental property of deep learning.

claim: Convolutional deep neural networks (DNN) are artificial neural networks that learn to approximate the underlying function that transforms input to associated output through multiple rounds of optimization.
source: Especially important are convolutional deep neural networks (DNN), artificial neural networks that learn to approximate the underlying function that transforms input to associated output through multiple rounds of optimization.
evidence: This describes the fundamental mechanism of DNNs based on established knowledge in machine learning.

claim: The strength of DNN is the ability to learn arbitrarily complex functions to best recognize particular aspects of the given input data and model complex nonlinear relationships.
source: The strength of DNN is the ability to learn arbitrarily complex functions to best recognize particular aspects of the given input data and model complex nonlinear relationships.
evidence: This describes a fundamental property of DNNs based on established knowledge in machine learning.

claim: The DNN is able to classify data into predefined classes based on the provided training labels.
source: The DNN is then able to classify data into predefined classes based on the provided training labels.
evidence: This describes the classification capability of DNNs based on established knowledge in machine learning.

claim: While the training of a DNN is generally a computationally intensive process, once trained the final model can easily be shared and used for making predictions at almost no computational cost to end-users.
source: While the training of a DNN is generally a computationally intensive process, once trained the final model can easily be shared and used for making predictions at almost no computational cost to end-users.
evidence: This describes a practical property of trained DNNs based on established knowledge in machine learning.

claim: DeepFRET is an all-inclusive analysis software with a pre-trained DNN at its core for rapid, objective, and accurate assessment of smFRET data.
source: Here we provide DeepFRET, an all-inclusive analysis software with a pre-trained DNN at its core, for a rapid, objective, and accurate assessment of smFRET data for quantifying biomolecular dynamics.
evidence: This describes the main contribution of the manuscript.

claim: DeepFRET operates with minimal crucial human intervention and requires only a threshold on the data quality confidence.
source: The fully automated analysis software operates with minimal crucial human intervention and requires only a threshold on the data quality confidence, as an initial step, to output detailed quantification of structural dynamic from raw images.
evidence: This describes a key feature of DeepFRET as implemented in the software.

claim: DeepFRET integrates and automates common smFRET analysis procedures from raw image analysis to production of publication-quality figures.
source: This is attained by an intuitive and user-friendly interface that integrates and automates common smFRET analysis procedures (Greenfeld et al., 2012; Hellenkamp et al., 2018; Hon and Gonzalez, 2019; Juette et al., 2016; Preus et al., 2015; Stella et al., 2018) from raw image analysis and background-corrected intensity trace extraction (Thomsen et al., 2019), to sophisticated trace classification, statistical analysis of single-molecule data and production of publication-quality figures of dynamic structural biology insights (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the capabilities of DeepFRET as implemented in the software.

claim: DeepFRET comes as a free-to-use standalone executable for both Windows and Mac users.
source: DeepFRET comes as a free-to-use standalone executable for both Windows and Mac users allowing end-users with limited programming skills to easily operate it.
evidence: This describes the software distribution format.

claim: A script-based version of DeepFRET implemented entirely in Python enables experts to adjust features pipelining the analysis specified for their needs.
source: A script-based version implemented entirely in Python enables experts to adjust features pipelining the analysis specified for their needs.
evidence: This describes an additional version of the software for expert users.

claim: The neural network model architecture used in DeepFRET is based on a deep convolutional neural network to recognize particular spatial features present in the data.
source: The neural network model architecture used here is based on a deep convolutional neural network to recognize particular spatial features present in the data.
evidence: This describes the technical architecture of the DeepFRET model.

claim: The DeepFRET model passes data through several layers of convolutions of different lengths and learns to recognize which particular elements of a sample are present at different length scales.
source: The model first passes the data through several layers of convolutions of different lengths, and in the process learns to recognize which particular elements of a sample are present at different length scales, to best classify it correctly.
evidence: This describes the technical mechanism of the DeepFRET model.

claim: Convolutional neural networks have previously been used to label time-series data such as electrocardiographs or electrical readouts in DNA sequencing.
source: This has previously been used to label time-series data such as electrocardiographs (Hannun et al., 2019) or electrical readouts in DNA sequencing (Wick et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published applications of CNNs.

claim: DeepFRET includes a long short-term memory (LSTM) layer after the convolutional layers to help the model learn temporality in the data.
source: Additionally, we added a long short-term memory (LSTM) layer after the convolutional layers, as this will also help the model to learn temporality in the data and propagate to the later frames the learned information (Karim et al., 2018; Oh et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes a technical feature of the DeepFRET model architecture, supported by citations.

claim: The DNN is pre-trained on 150,000 simulated traces that uniformly sample all possible FRET states, their respective lifetimes, occupancies, and transition pathways, as well as all possible noise levels.
source: The implemented DNN is pre-trained on 150,000 simulated traces that uniformly sample all possible FRET states, their respective lifetimes, occupancies, and transition pathways, as well as all possible noise levels, ensuring that the data represents all theoretically possible configurations (see Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5, Materials and methods for software and algorithms).
evidence: This describes the training data used for the DeepFRET model.

claim: DeepFRET does not require the selection of any direct initial guesses of FRET values or user-defined parameter pretraining.
source: As such DeepFRET does not require the selection of any direct initial guesses of FRET values or user-defined parameter pretraining.
evidence: This describes a key feature of DeepFRET's operation.

claim: DeepFRET treats both alternating laser excitation (ALEX) and non-ALEX FRET data.
source: We built DeepFRET to treat both alternating laser excitation (ALEX) and non-ALEX FRET data.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of DeepFRET as implemented in the software.

claim: DeepFRET imports raw microscope images and performs colocalization of the two channels to extract background corrected intensity traces.
source: DeepFRET imports raw microscope images and performs colocalization of the two channels, to extract background corrected intensity traces of DD (donor excitation; donor emission), DA (donor excitation; acceptor emission), their respective stoichiometry, and in the case of ALEX data, also AA (acceptor excitation; acceptor emission; see Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This describes the image processing capabilities of DeepFRET.

claim: DeepFRET can directly load and process previously-obtained time-traces ASCII format as exported from the iSMS software package.
source: Alternatively, one can directly load and process previously-obtained time-traces ASCII format as exported from the popular software package iSMS (Preus et al., 2015) without their associated videos.
evidence: This describes the data import capabilities of DeepFRET.

claim: For a given time trace the DNN predicts and outputs six softmaxed probabilities to each time frame, representing six categories: bleached, static smFRET, dynamic smFRET, aggregate, noisy, and scrambled.
source: For a given time trace the DNN predicts and outputs six softmaxed probabilities pi to each time frame (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplement 5 and Materials and methods), representing the six categories it has been trained to recognize: bleached (B), static smFRET within the experimental time frame (S), dynamic smFRET (D), aggregate (A), noisy (N), and all other types of non treatable data smFRET data defined here as scrambled (X) (Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplements 5 and 7).
evidence: This describes the output of the DeepFRET model, with reference to figures showing examples.

claim: Both static and dynamic traces are included for further analysis in DeepFRET.
source: Both static and dynamic traces are included for further analysis.
evidence: This describes the data selection criteria in DeepFRET.

claim: DeepFRET uses a sliding window to search for frames predicted to be bleached with >0.5 probability.
source: Given these probabilities, which sums to one, a simple sliding window then searches for frames predicted by the DNN to be bleached (pB >0.5, see (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 5–8) for evaluation accuracy, and blinking exclusion).
evidence: This describes the bleaching detection algorithm in DeepFRET.

claim: When bleaching is found, the rest of the trace is removed to exclude the photobleached frames from further analysis.
source: When bleaching is found, the rest of the trace is removed to exclude the photobleached frames part of a trace from further analysis.
evidence: This describes the data processing procedure in DeepFRET.

claim: DeepFRET requires traces to contain a minimum number of viable frames (set to 15 but adjustable).
source: If the trace still contains a minimum number of viable frames (here set to 15 but adjustable), the probabilities are summed up over all remaining time frames for each of the five remaining categories and divided by the number of frames for normalization (see Materials and methods and Figure 1c, Figure 1—figure supplements 5–8).
evidence: This describes a parameter in the DeepFRET analysis pipeline.

claim: The DeepFRET score represents the DNN model confidence that a trace is truly smFRET.
source: We define the summaries of the combined static and dynamic trace scores as the 'DeepFRET score', representing the DNN model confidence that a trace is truly smFRET.
evidence: This defines a key metric used in DeepFRET.

claim: If the DeepFRET score is above the user-defined threshold, the trace is accepted for subsequent analysis.
source: If the DeepFRET score is above the user-defined threshold, the trace is accepted for the subsequent analysis (see Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 8 and Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the trace selection criterion in DeepFRET.

claim: Subsequent analysis in DeepFRET involves two-channel fitting of idealized FRET traces using Hidden Markov modeling.
source: Subsequent analysis involves two-channel fitting of idealized FRET traces using Hidden Markov modeling HMM (using the open-source package pomegranate); data and statistical evaluation of the abundance of FRET states and lifetimes; application of correction factors; and transition density plots (see Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplements 6 and 9–11).
evidence: This describes the analysis capabilities of DeepFRET.

claim: The number of underlying FRET distributions is automatically determined using Bayesian information criterion (BIC) in DeepFRET.
source: The number of underlying FRET distributions is automatically determined using Bayesian information criterion (BIC), offering the unbiased analysis of distribution of biomolecular distances (see Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplements 6 and 9–11).
evidence: This describes a statistical method implemented in DeepFRET.

claim: All data can be directly exported in publication-quality figures or extracted as data for user specific analysis in DeepFRET.
source: All data can be directly exported in publication-quality figures or extracted as data for user specific analysis if required.
evidence: This describes the output capabilities of DeepFRET.

claim: 200 ground truth smFRET traces were simulated and merged with 5000 random, non-smFRET traces to test DeepFRET performance.
source: To test our DeepFRET performance in practice, we initially compared it with commonly used threshold values. To be on the safe site, we simulated 200 ground truth smFRET traces and merged them with a dataset containing 5000 random, non-smFRET traces (too noisy, aggregates of multiple molecules, aberrant single-molecule behavior, see Materials and methods for parameter descriptions).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for testing DeepFRET.

claim: Common procedures for pre-selecting valid smFRET data often rely on an initial automatic threshold based on anticorrelated signal, fluorophore bleaching, noise levels, or fluorophore stoichiometry.
source: Common procedures for pre-selecting valid data for treatment often rely on an initial automatic threshold for discarding this large fraction of non-smFRET data (see Figure 1a). This is based on any number of combinations of the anticorrelated signal of the donor and acceptor, fluorophore bleaching, noise levels, or certain ranges of fluorophore stoichiometry, if recorded using ALEX methods (Hellenkamp et al., 2018; Hohlbein et al., 2014; Juette et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2005; McKinney et al., 2006; Preus et al., 2015; van de Meent et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes common practices in smFRET analysis, supported by citations.

claim: Simple thresholding based on median stoichiometry and max intensity recovered a poorly-defined FRET distribution that does not recapitulate the underlying ground truth two-state conformational equilibrium.
source: We first removed photobleaching and then accepted or rejected traces based on commonly used thresholds of median stoichiometry and max intensity (but not anticorrelation, see Materials and methods) without any manual post-inspection of the data. Figure 2b displays ground truth distribution (green) and the distribution of the accepted traces (pink) for varying the above thresholds. We recovered a poorly-defined FRET distribution that even at the tightest threshold does not recapitulate the underlying ground truth two-state conformational equilibrium.
evidence: This describes experimental results comparing simple thresholding to ground truth, shown in Figure 2b.

claim: For simple thresholding, precision and recall remained around 0.22 and 0.40 in the best case.
source: We calculated the common model evaluation metrics 'precision' and 'recall' (see Materials and methods) to quantify the quality of the predictions. The precision and recall, though improved by tightening the threshold, remain around 0.22 and 0.40, in the best case for simple thresholding (Figure 2b).
evidence: This presents quantitative performance metrics for simple thresholding shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Out of 366 traces selected by simple thresholding, only 80 were true positive, while 286 were false positive and 120 false negative.
source: The fact that out of 366 selected traces only 80 were true positive, while 286 were false positive and 120 false negative, highlights the need for human intervention as many traces are indistinguishable with simple statistical characterization (selected examples are shown below the histograms [Figure 2b]).
evidence: This presents quantitative results for simple thresholding performance.

claim: DeepFRET allowed high-fidelity recovery of the underlying ground truth distribution reaching a precision of 0.91 when setting a DeepFRET score of 0.85.
source: DeepFRET, on the other hand, allowed the high-fidelity recovery of the underlying ground truth distribution reaching a precision of 0.91 when setting a DeepFRET score of 0.85 (Figure 2c) without the need for human intervention.
evidence: This presents quantitative performance results for DeepFRET shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Virtually identical FRET distributions matching the ground truth data are derived for a large fraction of DeepFRET score thresholds (0.5–0.85).
source: The virtually identical FRET distributions, matching the ground truth data, that are derived for a large fraction of score thresholds (0.5– 0.85) show no systematic biases originating from data evaluation and illustrate the minimum impact of human interventions when using DeepFRET (see Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the robustness of DeepFRET across different thresholds, shown in figures.

claim: DeepFRET correctly identified single or complex multistate FRET distributions reaching precision 0.91 as compared to just 0.22 for standard threshold setting.
source: As expected, the fidelity of DeepFRET pertained to correctly identifying single or complex multistate FRET distributions (see Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–2) reaching precision 0.91 as compared to just 0.22 for standard threshold setting in the absence of further human intervention.
evidence: This presents comparative performance metrics between DeepFRET and standard thresholding.

claim: Thresholding data with DeepFRET scores in the regime 0.8–0.9 appears optimal for maintaining sufficient and high-fidelity data.
source: Quantification of precision and recall of the selection for various DeepFRET score thresholds displays the tradeoffs in recovering a high fraction of useful data. Thresholding data with scores in the regime 0.8–0.9 appears optimal for maintaining sufficient and high-fidelity data (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) for the trace characteristics here.
evidence: This presents an analysis of optimal threshold selection based on precision-recall tradeoffs.

claim: A DeepFRET score threshold of 0.85 was employed as optimal for maintaining high precision at reasonable recall values.
source: Based on these data, we employed a DeepFRET score threshold of 0.85 as optimal for maintaining high precision at reasonable recall values.
evidence: This describes the threshold selection decision based on the data analysis.

claim: DeepFRET classified data in a fraction of the time required for data classification by human operators (~1 min for 10,000 traces on a normal laptop, as compared to potentially days for manually inspected traces).
source: This was achieved in a fraction of the time required for data classification by human operators (~1 min for 10,000 traces on a normal laptop, as compared to potentially days for manually inspected traces).
evidence: This presents timing comparison data between DeepFRET and manual classification.

claim: The high classification accuracy for the annotation of individual frames is highlighted by the clear diagonal feature in confusion matrices.
source: We quantified and displayed using confusion matrix the discordance between the ground truth data and the data selected and classified by DeepFRET (Figure 3). In the confusion matrices, displayed in Figure 3, each row represents the predicted classification of traces while each column represents the ground truth data. The high classification accuracy for the annotation of individual frames is highlighted by the clear diagonal feature.
evidence: This describes the confusion matrix results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Similar classification performance was found for a DNN trained on non-ALEX FRET (ALEX-disabled model).
source: We found similar classification performance for a DNN trained on non-ALEX FRET (by a DNN with only DD and DA inputs, which we will refer to as 'ALEX-disabled'; Figure 3 right panels) signifying the applicability of the DeepFRET approach to both ALEX and non-ALEX FRET data.
evidence: This presents comparative performance results for ALEX and non-ALEX models shown in Figure 3.

claim: The misclassification between static and dynamic smFRET traces consists of <3% dynamic traces being misclassified as static, for both model types.
source: The misclassification between static and dynamic smFRET traces is practically non-existent and consists of <3% dynamic traces being misclassified as static, for both model types.
evidence: This presents quantitative misclassification rates from the confusion matrix analysis.

claim: DeepFRET classified bleached or aggregated frames with 98% true positives for ALEX-FRET model (97% for the non-ALEX model).
source: DeepFRET was found to classify bleached or aggregated frames with a 98% the true positives for ALEX-FRET model enabled (97% for the non-ALEX model), whereas only 89% (and 83% for ALEX-disabled) of the scrambled traces were correctly classified (see also Figure 2—figure supplement 3 for a detailed breakdown of the precision and recall).
evidence: This presents quantitative classification accuracy for specific categories.

claim: 89% of scrambled traces were correctly classified by the ALEX-enabled model (83% for ALEX-disabled).
source: DeepFRET was found to classify bleached or aggregated frames with a 98% the true positives for ALEX-FRET model enabled (97% for the non-ALEX model), whereas only 89% (and 83% for ALEX-disabled) of the scrambled traces were correctly classified (see also Figure 2—figure supplement 3 for a detailed breakdown of the precision and recall).
evidence: This presents quantitative classification accuracy for scrambled traces.

claim: The model is trained with a noise contribution drawn from a normal distribution with σ uniformly distributed between 0.01 and 0.30.
source: We note that the model is trained with a noise contribution that is drawn from a normal distribution of varying width (σ uniformly distributed between 0.01 and 0.30, multiplied by the maximum single fluorophore intensity) with a small contribution of gamma-distributed noise.
evidence: This describes the training data characteristics for the DeepFRET model.

claim: Traces with σ above 0.25 are characterized by the employed DNN as 'noisy'.
source: As such, traces with σ above 0.25 are characterized by the employed DNN as 'noisy' (see Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the noise threshold used in the DeepFRET model.

claim: DeepFRET has a true-positive rate of 94% for smFRET traces and a true-negative rate of 94% for non-smFRET traces for the ALEX-enabled model.
source: By collapsing the per-trace confusion matrix into a binary 'smFRET' and 'non-smFRET' (as shown by the cross-lines in Figure 3b), DeepFRET was found to be very balanced overall, with a true-positive rate of 94% for smFRET traces, and a true-negative rate of non-smFRET traces (Figure 3c), resulting in an overall balanced classification accuracy of 94% for the ALEX-enabled model and 93% for the ALEX-disabled model.
evidence: This presents overall classification accuracy metrics shown in Figure 3.

claim: DeepFRET has an overall balanced classification accuracy of 94% for the ALEX-enabled model and 93% for the ALEX-disabled model.
source: By collapsing the per-trace confusion matrix into a binary 'smFRET' and 'non-smFRET' (as shown by the cross-lines in Figure 3b), DeepFRET was found to be very balanced overall, with a true-positive rate of 94% for smFRET traces, and a true-negative rate of non-smFRET traces (Figure 3c), resulting in an overall balanced classification accuracy of 94% for the ALEX-enabled model and 93% for the ALEX-disabled model.
evidence: This presents overall classification accuracy metrics shown in Figure 3.

claim: Three different human operators were compared to DeepFRET to evaluate the feasibility of manually inspecting and making decisions about smFRET examples.
source: We then compared the classification accuracy of DeepFRET to the accuracy of three different human operators working with smFRET to evaluate the feasibility of manually inspecting and making decisions about smFRET examples.
evidence: This describes the experimental design for comparing human and machine performance.

claim: 1000 ground truth traces were simulated, of which only 46 contained actual smFRET, for the human vs. machine comparison test.
source: We simulated 1000 ground truth traces, of which only 46 contained actual smFRET, at different, randomly chosen levels of noise.
evidence: This describes the test dataset used for human vs. machine comparison.

claim: The participants in the human vs. machine test were neither informed about the underlying distribution nor the true number of smFRET traces.
source: The participants were neither informed about the underlying distribution nor the true number of smFRET traces.
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions for the human vs. machine test.

claim: The average performance of human operators scored 0.76 ± 0.10 in precision and 0.83 ± 0.14 in recall.
source: The test revealed that the average performance of the human operators, scoring 0.76 ± 0.10 in precision and 0.83 ± 0.14 in recall, was close to the precision-recall curve of the DNN, on a relatively small dataset (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This presents quantitative performance metrics for human operators shown in Figure 3 supplement 1.

claim: One human participant scored slightly better than the DeepFRET model in both precision and recall but spent an average of 5 s per trace.
source: Notably, one participant scored slightly better than the model in both precision and recall but spent an average of 5 s per trace, which would significantly increase data treatment time, thus making this unfeasible in a high-throughput setting.
evidence: This presents comparative performance and timing data for one human participant.

claim: The large spread on precision and recall attained by human operators suggests a large possible spread in experimental outcomes.
source: The large spread on precision and recall attained by human operators on these data furthermore suggest a large possible spread in experimental outcomes and highlights the advantages of unifying, reproducible methodologies independent of human interventions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the variability observed in human operator performance.

claim: DeepFRET is equally good, or better, as careful manual inspection while offering orders of magnitude faster data evaluation.
source: We, therefore, argue that DeepFRET is equally good, or better, as careful manual inspection while offering orders of magnitude faster data evaluation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison data between DeepFRET and human operators.

claim: The model's generalizability was examined by evaluation on real experimental smFRET data previously published by Stella et al., 2018.
source: The model's generalizability was initially examined by evaluation on real experimental smFRET data previously published by us (Stella et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the validation approach using published experimental data.

claim: Pre-screening and manual inspection of the Stella et al. dataset resulted in 214 traces exhibiting smFRET.
source: The selected published dataset contains thousands of traces that included aggregates and incomplete labeled molecules, due to low labeling efficiency. Our pre-screening (using median stoichiometry and intensity distributions) and subsequent manual inspection of the data resulted in 214 traces to exhibit smFRET.
evidence: This describes the manual analysis results for the validation dataset.

claim: Applying the trained DeepFRET model with a threshold of 0.85 recovered 228 traces from the Stella et al. dataset, with a FRET distribution very closely matching manual selection.
source: Applying our trained model with a threshold of 0.85, without any other parameter tuning, recovered 228 traces, with a FRET distribution very closely matching manual selection (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This presents the DeepFRET results on real experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The total data evaluation time of DeepFRET is <50 ms per trace on a recent laptop.
source: The total data evaluation time of <50 ms per trace (on a recent laptop) free of human intervention highlights the potential of DeepFRET to rapidly and reliably evaluate high throughput smFRET data.
evidence: This presents timing performance data for DeepFRET.

claim: DeepFRET trace selection is deterministic and strictly relies on the score threshold, independent of potential human cognitive bias.
source: Most importantly, the trace selection is deterministic, strictly relies on the score threshold, and is thus independent of potential human cognitive bias.
evidence: This describes a key advantage of DeepFRET's automated approach.

claim: DeepFRET was compared to existing robust software packages iSMS, SPARTAN, ebFRET, and HAMMY.
source: To further evaluate the performance of DeepFRET we compared it to the existing, robust, and widely used software packages for classification and treatment of smFRET data, iSMS, and SPARTAN (Juette et al., 2016; Preus et al., 2015), as well as ebFRET and HAMMY that focus on the kinetic analysis (McKinney et al., 2006; van de Meent et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the comparative evaluation approach with citations to the compared software.

claim: For simulated data, 200 ground truth smFRET traces were merged with 1800 simulated, non-smFRET traces for software comparison.
source: For the simulated data, 200 ground truth smFRET traces were merged with 1800 simulated, non-smFRET traces and sorted by the various software packages.
evidence: This describes the test dataset used for software comparison.

claim: DeepFRET was found to sort traces at least similarly to, or better than, both SPARTAN and iSMS without any parameter tuning, closely matching the underlying ground truth distribution.
source: DeepFRET was found to sort traces at least similarly to, or better than, both SPARTAN and iSMS without any parameter tuning, closely matching the underlying ground truth distribution, while ebFRET and HAMMY would require further sorting by manual selection or additional software packages for optimal results (see Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This presents comparative performance results shown in Figure 4 supplement 3.

claim: All software packages (DeepFRET, SPARTAN, iSMS) were able to reproduce published FRET distributions from raw tif files with little discrepancy on experimental data from Kilic et al., 2018 and Hellenkamp et al., 2018.
source: We then compared the performance of the three software packages offering advanced sorting on experimental data from other groups (Kilic et al., 2018; Hellenkamp et al., 2018). To ensure proper testing, the performance was evaluated on both ALEX and non-ALEX data. Our data show that all software packages were able to reproduce published FRET distributions from raw tif files with a little discrepancy (see Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This presents comparative results on published experimental data shown in Figure 4 supplement 4.

claim: DeepFRET is provided as a standalone executable with simple and detailed instructions for non-machine learning experts and users without programming skills.
source: To ensure the facile operation of DeepFRET by non-machine learning experts and users without any programming skills, we provided a standalone executable along with simple and detailed instructions on how to use it (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the software distribution and documentation.

claim: DeepFRET implements and automates in a user-friendly platform all common procedures for smFRET analysis from raw image analysis to transition density plots.
source: DeepFRET implements and automates in a user-friendly and intuitive platform all common procedures for smFRET analysis: sophisticated raw image analysis from raw. tiff files; particle and signal detection and localization; pixel intensity extraction for each biomolecule on both spectral channels and background corrected fluorescence and FRET trace trajectories; automatic trace classification and sorting; unbiased analysis of number of FRET states based on BIC analysis; 2-channel fitting of idealized FRET traces using HMM analysis based on calculated number of states by BIC; data and statistical evaluation of abundance of FRET states and lifetimes; application of correction factors; and transition density plots (see Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplements 9–11).
evidence: This describes the comprehensive capabilities of DeepFRET software.

claim: DeepFRET offers interoperability and backward-compatible trace loading from .txt files exported from the iSMS software package.
source: DeepFRET furthermore offers interoperability and backward-compatible trace loading from. txt files exported from the popular iSMS software package.
evidence: This describes a compatibility feature of DeepFRET.

claim: The software can export all results to publication-ready quality figures and allows extraction of data for further user-specific downstream analysis.
source: The software can export all results to publication-ready quality figures and also allows the extraction of data for further user-specific downstream analysis if desired.
evidence: This describes the output capabilities of DeepFRET.

claim: The freely available open-source code allows expert users to adjust features pipelining the analysis depending on their needs.
source: The freely available open-source code and the underlying mathematical operations that are based on many commonly used packages (e.g. NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib) will allow expert users to adjust features pipelining the analysis depending on their needs (see Code Availability).
evidence: This describes the open-source nature and customizability of DeepFRET.

claim: The DNN model is trained using Keras/TensorFlow, one of the most popular frameworks for deep learning.
source: The DNN model is trained using Keras/TensorFlow, one of the most popular frameworks for deep learning.
evidence: This describes the technical implementation framework used for DeepFRET.

claim: DeepFRET provides the option for simulating new data with additional parameters offering the possibility of DNN model re-training.
source: While the DNN is pre-trained with DeepFRET, we also provide the option for simulating new data with additional parameters offering the possibility of DNN model re-training to meet the specialized needs of trained users (e.g. multicolor FRET).
evidence: This describes the extensibility of DeepFRET for expert users.

claim: A neural network classifier trained on purely simulated smFRET time-series accurately and efficiently recognizes and classifies smFRET both in simulated ground truth data and in a real-world dataset.
source: Our experiments show that a neural network classifier trained on purely simulated smFRET time-series accurately and efficiently recognizes and classifies smFRET both in simulated ground truth data and in a real-world dataset.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: DeepFRET classification accuracy consistently outperformed trace selection using commonly published thresholds.
source: DeepFRET classification accuracy consistently outperformed trace selection using commonly published thresholds.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comparative results presented in the manuscript.

claim: DeepFRET supersedes the selection accuracy of human operators and only requires a fraction of the time (minutes versus weeks if traces are manually selected).
source: Similarly, it supersedes the selection accuracy of human operators and importantly, only requiring a fraction of the time (minutes versus weeks if traces are manually selected).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the human vs. machine comparison results.

claim: DeepFRET's drastic reduction of analysis times will allow the acquisition of even larger datasets expanding the field for high throughput analysis.
source: Such a drastic reduction of analysis times will allow the acquisition of even larger datasets expanding the field for high throughput analysis and improving the robustness of conclusion.
evidence: This is a forward-looking inference about the impact of DeepFRET on the field.

claim: DeepFRET has potential to form a reference against which the quality of the data and the structural biology insights are benchmarked.
source: The fact that DeepFRET does so only requiring a score threshold, as a sole human intervention, demonstrates its strength as a novel smFRET analysis method and its potential to form a reference against which the quality of the data and the structural biology insights are benchmarked.
evidence: This is a forward-looking claim about the potential impact of DeepFRET on standardization.

claim: DeepFRET was found to perform accurately for both ALEX and non-ALEX smFRET data.
source: DeepFRET was found to perform accurately for both ALEX and non-ALEX smFRET data (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplements 3–4) highlighting its precise classification and applicability across laboratories and methods.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comparative results shown in Figure 4 and supplements.

claim: The limited effect of human operators on data selection illustrates DeepFRET's potential to contribute to the standardization of the field, increasing reproducibility across laboratories.
source: The limited effect of human operators on data selection on the other hand illustrates its potential to contribute to the standardization of the field, increasing reproducibility across laboratories.
evidence: This is an inference about the impact of DeepFRET on field standardization.

claim: DeepFRET, combined with the advent of commercial single-molecule instruments, will contribute in materializing smFRET as a robust mainstream toolkit for structural biology labs.
source: We anticipate that DeepFRET, combined with the advent of commercial single-molecule instruments, will contribute in materializing the smFRET as a robust mainstream toolkit for structural biology labs.
evidence: This is a forward-looking speculation about the impact of DeepFRET on the field.

claim: DeepFRET is currently trained and thoroughly tested to operate on 2-color ALEX and non-ALEX smFRET data.
source: DeepFRET is currently trained and thoroughly tested to operate on 2-color ALEX and non-ALEX smFRET data.
evidence: This describes the current scope of DeepFRET's capabilities.

claim: Other experimental techniques such as 3- and 4-color FRET, PIFE, MIET, or i-SET could be implemented in the future through additional simulation of training data with subsequent DNN re-training and software optimization.
source: Other experimental techniques such as 3- and 4-color FRET (Stein et al., 2011; Yoo et al., 2020), protein-induced fluorescence enhancement (PIFE; Hwang and Myong, 2014), metal-induced energy transfer (MIET; Chizhik et al., 2014) or intraparticle surface energy transfer (i-SET; Zhou et al., 2020) could be implemented in the future through additional simulation of training data with subsequent DNN re-training and software optimization (see Materials and methods and data availability for instructions).
evidence: This is a forward-looking speculation about potential extensions of DeepFRET, with citations to relevant techniques.

claim: The simulation of data in DeepFRET is based on the assumption that protein dynamics as observed by smFRET follows a Markov process.
source: The simulation of data in DeepFRET is based on the assumption that protein dynamics as observed by smFRET follows a Markov process.
evidence: This describes a fundamental assumption underlying the DeepFRET simulation approach.

claim: In its current version, DeepFRET operates on surface-immobilized particles only.
source: In its current version, DeepFRET operates on surface-immobilized particles only, however implementing single-particle tracking as described in Bohr et al., 2019 would allow simultaneous tracking and extraction of dynamics through smFRET on freely diffusing particles open up exciting possibilities, for example, live cell imaging with single-particletracking (Singh et al., 2020) and in vivo high throughput smFRET studies (White et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes a current limitation of DeepFRET with speculation about future extensions.

claim: DeepFRET's neural network is trained to operate for smFRET data but the approach of time-series classification and sequence annotation can be extended to other stochastic single-molecule trajectories.
source: DeepFRET's neural network is trained to operate for smFRET data but our approach of time-series classification and sequence annotation can conveniently be extended to consider a spectrum of stochastic single-molecule trajectories of individual turnovers including tracking (Bohr et al., 2019; Ferro et al., 2019; Lu et al., 1998; Persson et al., 2013), constant force measurements (Goldman et al., 2015) and blinking of individual molecules (Durisic et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2019) using either simulated or high-quality annotated experimental data for training.
evidence: This is a forward-looking speculation about potential extensions of the DeepFRET approach, with citations to relevant applications.

claim: The neural network of DeepFRET or similar approaches are expected to be a paradigm shift and enable new fully automated analysis methodologies related to biomolecular recognition, protein folding and dynamics, and super resolution.
source: Consequently, we expect the neural network of DeepFRET or similar approaches to be a paradigm shift and enable new fully automated analysis methodologies related to biomolecular recognition, protein folding and dynamics, and super resolution.
evidence: This is a forward-looking speculation about the broader impact of the DeepFRET approach.

claim: Such advances are paramount for increasing the breadth and impact of single-molecule studies to be fully exploited in structural biology.
source: Such advances are paramount for increasing the breadth and impact of single-molecule studies to be fully exploited in structural biology.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about the importance of automated analysis methods for the field.

claim: Deep learning requires large amounts of diverse data in order to generalize well to unseen data.
source: Deep learning requires large amounts of diverse data in order to generalize well to unseen data.
evidence: This describes a fundamental property of deep learning based on established knowledge in machine learning.

claim: A method was developed to generate thousands of ground truth traces to cover every type of empirically observed trace.
source: We have developed a method to generate the required thousands of ground truth traces to cover every type of empirically observed trace, with a dedicated user interface option (Figure 1—figure supplements 2 and 6).
evidence: This describes a methodological contribution of the manuscript.

claim: The trace generation algorithm includes generation of TIRF-microscopy smFRET traces of ALEX or non-ALEX data with tunable parameters.
source: This algorithm includes the generation of TIRF-microscopy smFRET traces of ALEX or non-ALEX data. The traces sample any given FRET value with tunable dye photobleaching lifetime, signal noise, dye blinking, donor bleedthrough, aggregates (i.e. more than one donor/acceptor fluorophore) of any given size, as well as a 'scrambling' feature, to account for fluorophore phenomena that could not be classified as stemming from smFRET.
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the trace generation algorithm.

claim: For training the model, 250,000 traces of 300 frames each were randomly initially generated with specified parameters.
source: With these parameters, directly applicable as input for the algorithm (see Code availability), we randomly initially generated 250.000 traces of 300 frames each of randomized configurations.
evidence: This describes the training data generation process.

claim: Data was under-sampled to balance the labels based on the first frame of each trace, resulting in approximately 150,000 traces.
source: We then under-sampled data to balance the labels (as neural network classifiers perform worse if trained on highly class-imbalanced datasets) based on the first frame of each trace. This resulted in approximately 150,000 traces, roughly equally distributed over the five possible classes (bleaching being present in most traces naturally ends up accounting for a higher fraction of the overall frames).
evidence: This describes the data preprocessing for model training.

claim: 80% of the balanced data was used for training the classifier and the remaining 20% for validation.
source: We used 80% for training the classifier and the remaining 20% for validation.
evidence: This describes the train-validation split used for model development.

claim: An additional test set with 33,000 new traces was generated and under-sampled to roughly 20,000 traces for statistical analysis.
source: After the training procedure, we generated an additional test set with 33.000 new traces and under-sampled it as previously, to roughly 20.000 traces, and based our statistical analysis on those alone.
evidence: This describes the independent test set used for model evaluation.

claim: Only the raw features DD, DA, and AA were supplied to the model (or only DD and DA for the non-ALEX-enabled model).
source: We supplied only the raw features DD, DA, and AA to the model (or only DD and DA for the non-ALEX-enabled model), where for each trace, signals were normalized to the max of all signals in that trace to preserve the relative intensities between donor and acceptor.
evidence: This describes the input features used for the DeepFRET model.

claim: Signals were normalized to the max of all signals in each trace to preserve the relative intensities between donor and acceptor.
source: We supplied only the raw features DD, DA, and AA to the model (or only DD and DA for the non-ALEX-enabled model), where for each trace, signals were normalized to the max of all signals in that trace to preserve the relative intensities between donor and acceptor.
evidence: This describes the normalization procedure used for model input.

claim: Predictions done on individual smFRET traces are fully independent from every other in a given experiment, and also independent of non-standardized instrument intensity units.
source: In this way, predictions done on individual smFRET traces are fully independent from every other in a given experiment, and also independent of non-standardized instrument intensity units (i.e. 'arbitrary units').
evidence: This describes an important property of the DeepFRET model resulting from the normalization approach.

claim: An LSTM-RNN classifier was implemented in Keras with TensorFlow as backend.
source: An LSTM-RNN (long short-term memory recurrent neural network) classifier was implemented in Keras with TensorFlow as backend.
evidence: This describes the technical implementation of the DeepFRET model.

claim: The structure of the network was inspired by a recent sequence classifier for ECG time-series.
source: The structure of the network (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) was inspired by a recent sequence classifier for ECG time-series (Hannun et al., 2019) that employs both skip connections and batch normalization as means to prevent overfitting.
evidence: This describes the architectural inspiration for the DeepFRET model, with citation.

claim: The global pooling layer was replaced with stride-1 max pooling layers, and a bidirectional LSTM layer was added before the final fully connected layer.
source: Here we replaced the global pooling layer with stride-1 max pooling layers, and added a bidirectional LSTM layer before the final fully connected layer, which we found lead to more temporally causal and context-sensitive predictions (e.g. if the model spots multiple bleaching steps in the beginning of a trace, this information is propagated throughout, so the whole trace can be confidently marked as aggregated).
evidence: This describes modifications made to the base architecture and their effects.

claim: The model loss was minimized in batches of 32 samples with the Adam optimizer using default parameters and learning rate of 0.001.
source: The model loss was minimized in batches of 32 samples with the Adam optimizer, using the default parameters and the default learning rate of 0.001.
evidence: This describes the training hyperparameters used for the DeepFRET model.

claim: The learning rate was decreased by a factor of 10 if validation loss showed no improvement over two consecutive epochs.
source: The learning rate was decreased by a factor of 10 if validation loss showed no improvement over two consecutive epochs.
evidence: This describes the learning rate schedule used during training.

claim: Training was stopped early if no improvement in the validation loss was observed over five consecutive epochs.
source: The training was stopped early if no improvement in the validation loss was observed over five consecutive epochs.
evidence: This describes the early stopping criterion used during training.

claim: A sliding window is employed where at least 4 out of 7 frames must be marked as bleached with >0.5 probability by the model for bleaching detection.
source: In order to avoid having single-frame bleaching triggering the remainder of the trace being marked as bleached, we employ a sliding window over the whole trace. In each window, at least 4 out of 7 frames must be marked as bleached with >0.5 probability by the model.
evidence: This describes the bleaching detection algorithm used in DeepFRET.

claim: If bleaching happens faster than the first 15 frames, the whole trace is classified as bleached, regardless of model classification.
source: Additionally, if bleaching happens faster than the first 15 frames, the whole trace is classified as bleached, regardless of model classification, as the DeepFRET score would otherwise end up being artificially inflated (see below).
evidence: This describes a special case handling in the bleaching detection algorithm.

claim: The label of traces was changed to 'noisy' if the initial noise was drawn from a normal distribution with σ above 0.25.
source: We changed the label of traces to 'noisy' if the initial noise was drawn from a normal(μ = 0, σ) with σ above 0.25.
evidence: This describes the noise threshold criterion used for labeling training data.

claim: Traces above a noise level of 0.25 could no longer statistically be approximated as normally distributed by D'Agostino-Pearson two-sided test for normality.
source: Traces above this level of noise could no longer statistically be approximated as normally distributed by D'Agostino-Pearson two-sided test for normality (Figure 1—figure supplement 4; which is a requirement for fitting the correct number of FRET states in a trace, using a mixture model).
evidence: This provides statistical justification for the noise threshold, shown in Figure 1 supplement 4.

claim: DeepFRET fits traces using the pomegranate implementation of the Baum-Welch algorithm.
source: We fit the traces using the pomegranate implementation of the Baum-Welch algorithm (Schreiber, 2018).
evidence: This describes the HMM implementation used in DeepFRET, with citation.

claim: The Hidden Markov model was verified on externally available data from the kinSoft challenge, as well as simulated data produced within DeepFRET.
source: The Hidden Markov model was verified on externally available data from the kinSoft challenge, as well as simulated data produced within DeepFRET.
evidence: This describes the validation approach for the HMM implementation.
